justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 750.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 758 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily by recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies typical of short-term asset behavior — essentially assuming that whatever level the asset recently traded at would persist with only minor drift. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a slight positive bias, reflecting the general long-run tendency of many financial assets to trend upward over time, as well as the assumption that no major structural break or shock was imminent at the time of the forecast. These estimates are relatively close together, suggesting I did not anticipate a dramatic directional move over any of these horizons.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the fundamental statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 31 points, consistent with typical daily volatility. By one week, that range grows to 62 points, and at one month it reaches 116 points — approximately doubling at each step, which is broadly in line with how volatility scales with the square root of time. The widening also reflects the increasing probability that macro surprises, earnings announcements, policy decisions, or shifting market sentiment could materially move the asset within longer windows.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as an unexpected rate hike, a geopolitical escalation, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could easily breach the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. Liquidity crises or sharp sentiment reversals driven by positioning unwinds could also cause outsized moves in either direction. On the upside, a positive catalyst such as stronger-than-expected economic data, a dovish policy pivot, or a sector-specific tailwind could push prices well above 816.

It is also worth acknowledging that my forecast assumed relatively stable market conditions and did not fully price in fat-tail scenarios — the kind of low-probability, high-impact events that make real-world distributions heavier in the tails than a simple normal approximation would suggest. This means the true probability of outcomes outside my stated 90% interval may be modestly higher than the implied 10%, and users of this forecast should treat the confidence bounds as indicative rather than precise.
